item.content:encoded:
Cricket-India hold off West Indies to take 2-1 series lead in third T20 Reuters | Updated: 11-10-2026 23:21 IST | Created: 11-10-2026 23:21 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

India beat West Indies by 14 runs on Sunday in Indore to take a 2-1 lead in the five-match Twenty20 International series. Chasing 224 for victory, West Indies suffered an early setback when Arshdeep Singh dismissed captain Shai Hope for five after he missed a swipe at a delivery that jagged back on to his stumps. Shimron Hetmyer kept the visitors in the hunt with a brisk 43 off 26 balls before spinner Naman Dhir broke the stand, while Axar Patel removed Rovman Powell to leave West Indies struggling to match the mounting required rate. Quentin Sampson and Sherfane Rutherford briefly revived the chase, but West Indies could not sustain the momentum as wickets fell regularly in the closing overs and they finished on 209-7. Arshdeep was India's standout bowler with 3-44 as the hosts defended a formidable 223 after being asked to bat. India recovered from the early loss of Sanju Samson, who fell for just three to Shamar Joseph, through a 108-run partnership for the second wicket between Abhishek Sharma and Ishan Kishan. Sharma dominated the scoring with an explosive 69 off 30 balls, while Kishan contributed 37. However, the hosts lost momentum when Kishan's dismissal triggered a middle-order collapse. The platform laid by Sharma ultimately proved decisive, allowing the lower order to keep the scoreboard moving and lift India to 223 before they were bowled out off the final delivery of the innings. The teams meet again in the fourth Twenty20 International in Hyderabad on Wednesday.

item.content:encoded:
Saudi Arabia reports injuries in new attack at Riyadh airport, day after strike kills 13 Reuters | Updated: 11-10-2026 23:19 IST | Created: 11-10-2026 23:19 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility for Saturday's strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, as Saudi authorities reported people were injured in a new attack on the airport on Sunday. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said an "unidentified projectile" had targeted Riyadh's international airport Terminal 4 on Sunday, causing a fire. An unspecified number of people were injured, the Saudi civil aviation authority said, adding it was still assessing the damage. The coalition also said Saudi air defences had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport. The strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi defence capabilities as the kingdom wages an air campaign against the Houthis to support a ground war in Yemen by the Yemeni government against the Iran-aligned group. The airport has been closed since Saturday's attack. However, a long-planned international energy conference went ahead in Riyadh on Sunday as planned. HOUTHIS CLAIM RESPONSIBILITY FOR OTHER ATTACKS In a televised speech on Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for Saturday's attack and also said the group had attacked the airport in Dammam in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province and two facilities of Saudi oil giant Saudi Aramco. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation. Reuters has reached out to the Saudi media office and to Aramco for comment. The Houthis earlier on Sunday had renewed their warning to airlines, airport workers, and travellers against using Saudi airports. "We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions," the group said. 'WORSE IS YET TO COME,' HOUTHIS WARN Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month. The Houthis said on Sunday that Saudi Arabia carried out 124 air strikes in Yemen in the past 24 hours, including the capital Sanaa and the group's stronghold Saada. Yemen's Houthi-run foreign ministry said that further Saudi military action in Yemen would trigger a stronger response, adding that its actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity. "Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the ministry said in statements carried by Houthi-run Al Masirah television. US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war on Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. INTERNATIONAL ENERGY CONFERENCE STILL GOING AHEAD The five-day conference of international energy organizations WPC Energy opened as planned on Sunday at a convention centre some 10 km (6 miles) from the airport. Meanwhile, a ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum also went ahead on Sunday, with its plenary session to be held behind closed doors, according to a media advisory. No further details were immediately available and it was not clear which ministers joined the meeting. Italy's energy minister, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, whose country was co-hosting the event, had said on Friday he would participate remotely via video link. German officials were trying to organise a return flight for Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, who was in Riyadh to attend the WPC conference and ministers' meeting. She was supposed to return to Berlin on Monday but the ministry said it appeared likely that her flight would not be able to take off due to the closure of the airport and alternatives were being considered. Separately, Saudi authorities notified parents that in-person classes at all schools in Riyadh would be suspended and shifted to remote learning from Sunday until Thursday for all students, teachers and administrative staff. In Saturday's attack, the third on Riyadh's airport in a week, the dead included four Saudis, two Bangladeshis and nationals of the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, Saudi authorities said. India's embassy in Riyadh said on Sunday one of its citizens injured in the attack had died, adding to the initial death toll of 12. Four people were killed in the two previous attacks on the airport earlier in the week. One of the attacks also caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.

item.content:encoded:
US threatens to block arms for Ukraine over refinery attacks, FT reports Reuters | Updated: 11-10-2026 23:19 IST | Created: 11-10-2026 23:19 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The US is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons in order to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing officials in Europe. The officials, who received calls from US officials or were briefed on them, said that the US was lobbying European capitals and Kyiv to try to end the attacks on Russian oil refineries, the report added. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The message from the US included threats to cut off intelligence sharing and Purl (the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism for procuring US weapons for Ukraine, the report added. "They are calling Kyiv . ... They are calling everyone [in Europe]," said an official who received a call from a US defence official, as per the report. The report comes after US President Donald Trump made a surprise announcement on Sunday of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that he said was "effective immediately," but Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he was still waiting to see details of the deal. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote.

Mexico's Sheinbaum urges coastal residents to remain indoors as Hurricane Simon nears coast Reuters | Updated: 11-10-2026 23:08 IST | Created: 11-10-2026 23:08 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

MEXICO CITY, Oct 11 - Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum urged residents along the country's Pacific coast to remain indoors on Sunday as powerful Category 4 Hurricane Simon approached Mexico's west-central coast, threatening destructive winds, dangerous storm surges and potentially deadly flooding. Simon was located about 65 miles (105 km) west-northwest of the port city of Manzanillo, in Colima state, with maximum sustained winds of 145 mph (230 kph), the US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said in its latest advisory at 9 a.m. local time. The hurricane was moving north-northwest at 11 kph (7 mph), with its center about 140 km (85 miles) south-southeast of Cabo Corrientes, in neighboring Jalisco state. "With the approaching impact of Category 4 Hurricane Simon, we urge residents of coastal municipalities in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to remain sheltered until authorities officially declare that the danger has passed," Sheinbaum said in a post on X. She said precautionary evacuations to safer areas were continuing and urged residents to stay off the streets and follow civil protection instructions. The NHC said Simon was expected to move very near Mexico's west-central coast later on Sunday and remain close to the coast on Monday, although forecast uncertainty remained over whether the center would cross inland or remain just offshore. Even without a direct landfall, dangerous storm surges, large destructive waves and damaging winds were likely along portions of Mexico's west-central coast, the forecaster warned. Mexico's National Civil Protection Coordination (CNPC) placed 28 municipalities in Jalisco and Colima under its highest cyclone alert level, while another 93 municipalities were under a high alert level, according to civil protection bulletins. Puerto Vallarta's international airport has temporarily closed, while authorities have suspended nonessential activities and opened emergency shelters in threatened coastal communities. The NHC warned that heavy rainfall through Monday could trigger life-threatening flooding and mudslides, particularly in mountainous areas. Simon intensified rapidly into a Category 4 hurricane on Saturday, prompting authorities to deploy military personnel, emergency workers and civil protection teams to vulnerable coastal communities. The storm comes a week after Hurricane Polo struck Mexico's Baja California Peninsula as a Category 2 hurricane, toppling trees and utility poles and flooding streets.
